metadata.name: Acute appendicitis
metadata.emergency_level: EMERGENCY - a common surgical abdomen; perforation causes peritonitis/sepsis
metadata.severity: Serious - requires urgent surgical assessment; perforation increases morbidity

overview.short_description: Acute inflammation of the appendix, the commonest surgical emergency, classically with peri-umbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa, requiring urgent assessment and usually appendicectomy.
overview.detailed_description: Appendicitis is a leading cause of the acute abdomen. Presentation can be atypical (children, elderly, pregnancy). The primary-care role is early recognition and prompt referral for surgical assessment - NOT to exclude it in the community. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by inflammatory markers and imaging (ultrasound/CT). Delay risks perforation, peritonitis and sepsis.
overview.pathophysiology: Luminal obstruction (faecolith, lymphoid hyperplasia) causes distension, bacterial overgrowth, mucosal ischaemia and inflammation; progression leads to necrosis and perforation with localised abscess or generalised peritonitis. Visceral pain (peri-umbilical) becomes somatic/localised (right iliac fossa) as the parietal peritoneum is involved.
overview.etiology: Appendiceal luminal obstruction and infection; sometimes no clear cause.
overview.natural_history: Progresses over hours-days from inflammation to perforation if untreated; some mild cases may resolve/recur.
overview.prognosis: Excellent with timely surgery; worse with perforation/delay, especially at extremes of age.

prevalence.value: Very common; lifetime risk of appendicitis is significant (a few percent).

incidence.value: Peaks in the second-third decades; occurs at any age.

mortality.value: Low with prompt treatment; higher with perforation/sepsis or delayed presentation.

epidemiology.age_groups: Most common in children/young adults; atypical and higher-risk in the very young and elderly.

risk_factors.pregnancy: Appendicitis in pregnancy has atypical location and higher risk - low threshold for assessment.

chief_complaints.complaint: Abdominal pain moving to the right lower abdomen

symptoms.symptom: Peri-umbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa

symptoms.importance: Very common - its absence makes appendicitis a little less likely
Vomiting before pain suggests another cause

symptoms.symptom: Right iliac fossa tenderness/guarding (McBurney's point), rebound
symptoms.importance: Key examination sign of localised peritonism

symptoms.symptom: Generalised abdominal pain/rigidity, high fever, unwell (perforation/peritonitis)

negative_findings.finding: No RIF tenderness, pain-free, eating normally, normal inflammatory markers
negative_findings.why_important: Makes appendicitis less likely (but does not fully exclude - reassess if progressing)

history_questions.question: Where did the pain start and where is it now?
Any loss of appetite, nausea/vomiting, and did vomiting come before or after the pain?
history_questions.why_ask: Anorexia is common; vomiting-before-pain suggests another cause

history_questions.question: For women: last menstrual period, pregnancy possibility, and gynaecological symptoms?
How severe/progressive is it, and any high fever or feeling very unwell?

physical_examination.examination: Abdominal examination (RIF tenderness, guarding, rebound, Rovsing's sign)
physical_examination.expected_finding: Localised RIF peritonism; generalised peritonitis if perforated

physical_examination.examination: Temperature, pulse, and signs of sepsis
physical_examination.expected_finding: Low-grade fever; sepsis features indicate perforation

laboratory_tests.expected_result: Raised white cell count and CRP (normal markers reduce but do not exclude)

imaging.imaging_type: Ultrasound (first-line in children/pregnancy/young women) or CT abdomen
imaging.when_needed: To confirm the diagnosis and assess complications when uncertain
imaging.expected_findings: Enlarged non-compressible appendix, wall thickening, fat stranding, abscess/perforation

other_diagnostic_tests.biopsy: Histology of the removed appendix confirms the diagnosis
other_diagnostic_tests.scoring: Clinical scores (e.g., Alvarado) support decision-making but do not replace assessment

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Primarily clinical: characteristic history (migrating RIF pain, anorexia, nausea) with RIF tenderness/peritonism, supported by raised inflammatory markers and imaging (ultrasound/CT) where used. Scores (e.g., Alvarado) aid risk stratification. Definitive diagnosis is often at surgery/histology.

diagnostic_scores.value: Alvarado score and paediatric appendicitis scores stratify likelihood.

differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: When was your last period and could you be pregnant?
Any diarrhoea or recent cold, with more diffuse pain?
Any burning on urination or loin-to-groin pain?

differential_diagnosis.disease: Other surgical causes (Meckel's, Crohn's, perforated ulcer, diverticulitis)
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Any features pointing to another surgical cause?

diagnostic_questions.question: For women of reproductive age: could you be pregnant (ectopic)?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Positive pregnancy test with pain -> emergency gynaecology assessment

diagnostic_questions.question: Did the pain start centrally and move to the right lower abdomen, with loss of appetite?
diagnostic_questions.interpretation: Migrating RIF pain + RIF tenderness -> urgent surgical referral

next_best_question.question: Is there RIF tenderness/peritonism, could she be pregnant, and are there signs of sepsis/perforation?
next_best_question.expected_answers: Localised appendicitis vs mimic vs perforation
next_best_question.branching_logic: Suspected appendicitis -> urgent same-day surgical referral (do not exclude in the community); pregnancy possible -> exclude ectopic; sepsis/peritonitis -> emergency admission

next_best_test.why: Appendicitis is a surgical emergency - refer, do not attempt to exclude in primary care

red_flags.finding: Generalised abdominal rigidity/peritonitis, high fever, tachycardia, hypotension (perforation/sepsis)
red_flags.immediate_action: Emergency - resuscitate and urgent surgical admission

red_flags.finding: Positive pregnancy test with abdominal pain
Rapidly worsening or severe localised pain with peritonism
Very young child or elderly/immunocompromised with abdominal pain
red_flags.immediate_action: Low threshold for urgent assessment (atypical/high-risk presentations)

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Any suspected appendicitis - urgent same-day surgical assessment.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: Not applicable (this is an acute condition).
referral_criteria.emergency_referral: Peritonitis/sepsis, suspected perforation, or ectopic pregnancy.

initial_management.supportive_care: In primary care: recognise and REFER urgently; keep nil by mouth; analgesia and safety-net while arranging transfer; do not give antibiotics that mask signs without surgical input.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Analgesia and IV fluids; Peri-operative/pathway antibiotic; Non-operative antibiotic strategy. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: WSES_APPENDICITIS_2025.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Not applicable acutely; post-operative recovery advice.
initial_management.follow_up: Surgical follow-up; histology review (occasionally reveals other pathology).
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Hospital management: IV fluids, analgesia, and antibiotics; APPENDICECTOMY (laparoscopic) is the standard treatment; selected uncomplicated cases may be managed with antibiotics under specialist care. Abscess may need drainage.

patient_education.home_advice: Appendicitis is a surgical emergency. The pain often starts around the belly button and moves to the lower-right tummy, with loss of appetite and feeling sick. It needs urgent hospital assessment - usually an operation to remove the appendix - because a burst appendix is dangerous. If you or your child has worsening tummy pain that settles in the lower-right side, especially with fever or vomiting, get medical help urgently. Do not just take painkillers and wait.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: التهاب الزائدة حالة طارئة جراحية. يبدأ الألم غالباً حول السرّة ثم ينتقل إلى أسفل يمين البطن، مع فقدان الشهية والغثيان. يحتاج تقييماً عاجلاً في المستشفى - عادةً عملية لاستئصال الزائدة - لأن انفجارها خطير. إذا أصابك أو أصاب طفلك ألم بطن متزايد يستقرّ في أسفل اليمين، خاصةً مع حرارة أو قيء، فاطلب المساعدة الطبية عاجلاً. لا تكتفِ بالمسكّنات والانتظار.
patient_education.warning_signs: Worsening/persistent right-lower abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, a rigid painful tummy, or feeling very unwell - seek emergency care.

evidence.evidence_level: High for surgical management; growing evidence for antibiotics-first in selected uncomplicated cases.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by WSES_APPENDICITIS_2025; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.
evidence.legacy_guideline_strength_pre_v13: Strong - surgical association guidance (e.g., WSES), NICE.

limitations: Guidelines require individual clinical judgement and may differ by country, formulary and antimicrobial resistance.
The evidence audit verifies traceability and major safety structure; it does not certify every narrative sentence.
No medication should be selected or dosed without patient-specific contraindication and interaction checking.

treatment_guidance.treatment_goal: Recognise a surgical emergency, provide analgesia/resuscitation and select surgery versus non-operative care in hospital.
treatment_guidance.legacy_narrative_summary: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): Analgesia and IV fluids; Peri-operative/pathway antibiotic; Non-operative antibiotic strategy. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: WSES_APPENDICITIS_2025.
required_history_before_any_medication: age and weight where dosing is weight- or age-dependent
pregnancy or breastfeeding status when relevant
documented drug allergies and the exact reaction
all prescribed, OTC, herbal and recreational substances
major cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal and bleeding history
non_drug_measures: Nil-by-mouth and resuscitation decisions belong to the acute surgical team.

medication_options.when_to_consider: After urgent assessment; analgesia should not be withheld solely to preserve signs
medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

avoid_if: severe active liver disease or prior serious reaction
use_caution_if: heavy alcohol use, malnutrition, low body weight, or concomitant paracetamol-containing products
monitoring: total daily exposure and clinical response

avoid_if: active gastrointestinal bleeding/ulcer, serious NSAID allergy, or NSAID-triggered asthma
use_caution_if: chronic kidney disease, heart failure, hypertension, anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy, older age, pregnancy, or dehydration
monitoring: renal function, blood pressure, oedema and gastrointestinal bleeding symptoms when clinically indicated

medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.
